Visual Checks That Narrow Down the Leak

A wet meter box can point to a service-line leak; a dry one does not rule one out. Visual checks can locate exposed drips and fixture faults, but they cannot reveal leaks underground or inside walls. Those may require acoustic detection or flow monitoring.

Start at the meter box and visible connections, then check indoor fixtures and irrigation. Note where water appears and whether the spot is wet when the fixtures and irrigation are off. This helps narrow down the source, but the utility's responsibility for the meter or service line depends on local rules.
Visual Checks by Location and Sign of Leak
Check location
What to look for
What it points to
Meter pit or box
Standing water, soft or muddy soil, green patch on lawn
Possible leak at the service connection or meter couplings
Meter couplings and union nuts
Drips, mineral crust, wet gasket
Possible failing connection seal
Meter valve stems
Water at the stem, stiff or weeping handle
Possible worn valve packing
Toilet tank
Food colouring appears in bowl within 15 to 30 minutes
Flapper or fill valve may not be sealing
Water heater base and pan
Rust, pooling water, drip at the temperature-pressure valve
Possible heater or fitting leak
Supply lines and appliance hoses
Bulges, wet cabinet floor, drips at fittings
Possible hose or fitting failure
Irrigation valves and boxes
Wet spots, flow with all zones off
Possible zone valve that will not seal

For a toilet check, add food colouring to the tank, do not flush, and inspect the bowl after 15 to 30 minutes. If colour appears, the flapper or fill valve may be letting water through. At the water heater, inspect the pan and temperature-pressure valve. A leak there does not by itself prove the tank has failed.
A dry floor proves nothing. Pressurised water can escape into soil, wall cavities, or a toilet bowl without leaving a visible puddle.
Check irrigation with every zone off. Constant flow or a wet valve box can indicate a valve that is not sealing. Photograph each finding with the time, especially if you are disputing a bill.
Temporary Fixes Until a Plumber Arrives
Close the shutoff you're sure of. Don't remove meter seals, pull a meter, or tamper with utility equipment. You'll void clean testing and turn a repair into a billing fight.
That's the warning that matters most here. A stopgap should slow loss and protect finishes, not rewrite the evidence. Photograph the register before and after you touch anything.
Safest Fixes First
Running toilet:
Close the fixture isolation valve. Lift the flapper, clear grit from the seat, and replace a worn, curled flapper if you've got the right part.
Dripping meter coupling:
Snug the union nut slightly if it's clearly loose. Don't overtighten, since you can crack a fitting or crush a gasket.
Weeping valve stem:
Tighten the packing nut a quarter turn at most. If the valve still weeps or won't hold, stop and call the utility.
Water heater pan filling:
Shut the cold supply and turn the heater off. Put towels or a shallow pan down and keep people away from electrical components.

Meter pits need restraint. Pump standing water only if you can do it safely from above and you're authorised to access it. Don't climb into a pit or confined space, don't reach into water near electrical gear, and don't guess which valve belongs to the utility.

For a large leak with no working shutoff, close the curb stop only if you can reach it safely and you're allowed to operate it. Otherwise call the utility emergency line and protect flooring, documents, and electrical outlets while you wait.
What Not to Do
No hammering valves:
You'll break a stem that's already seized.
No tape on pressurised joints:
Pipe tape won't hold a live leak and hides the failure point.
No chemicals in the pit:
They contaminate the work area and solve nothing.
No forced handles:
A stiff valve that snaps leaves you with no isolation at all.
Stop point:
If you can't name the valve, who owns it, and what it shuts off, don't turn it.

Write down what you closed, when you closed it, and whether register movement stopped. That short note helps the plumber and protects you if the utility later asks why consumption changed mid-investigation.
Leak Detection Sensors and Alert Thresholds

A property can show a steady overnight flow even when no one is using water. A continuous meter reading helps distinguish a likely leak from a single appliance cycle, and shows whether the meter itself is registering flow.

children.text: Set the Baseline Before the Alarm
Choose a low-demand period.
Use overnight hours or another time when the property is normally quiet.
Record the baseline.
Note expected overnight flow, including equipment such as ice makers or softeners.
Set a practical alert.

For example, trigger an alert if flow stays above the established baseline for three consecutive hours. Adjust the duration if scheduled equipment runs overnight, and use a lower threshold for a vacant property.
Verify the reading.
Compare the meter's register with the alert, then check likely fixtures and equipment before assigning the loss to a pipe, suite, or meter.

The three-hour setting is a starting example, not a universal rule. A short window catches smaller leaks sooner but can trigger on normal cycles; a longer window reduces nuisance alerts but delays response.
After a repair, compare the readings before and after. If flow remains above baseline, keep investigating rather than treating the alert as resolved. For a comparison of monitoring options, see
how water leak detection sensors work in submetered buildings
The video below shows how continuous alerts can prompt inspection before the next monthly bill.
What Each Sensor Catches and Misses
Smart meters
can reveal abnormal continuous demand, provided the baseline is sound and each meter is mapped to the right suite.
Acoustic sensors
can help locate leaks in buried or concealed pressurised pipes, but cost more per monitoring point and need setup for the pipe material.
Floor pucks
under sinks, washers, or heaters alert after water reaches the sensor.
Pressure-decay tests
check an isolated section at one point in time; they do not provide continuous monitoring.

Keep common-area and suite readings separate so an alert can be traced to the correct area and responsible party. A sensor signals where to investigate; it does not, by itself, prove who owes for the water.
When to Replace a Leaking Water Meter
A high bill can come from a plumbing leak, a misread meter, or a mismatch between the meter and the unit it serves. Replace the meter only when inspection or a formal test supports that decision.

Meters can under-register, stop, or record inaccurately. A high bill alone does not prove a meter is faulty. Utilities may test meters at several flow rates, since a meter can perform differently at low and high flows. Accuracy limits depend on the applicable utility rules and test standards, so use the utility's stated criteria rather than assuming one threshold applies everywhere.

A passing meter with continued high readings points to other causes. Check for cross-connections, mislabelled suites, shared piping, or common-area lines assigned to the wrong meter. Replacing a meter without checking these can leave the billing problem unresolved.

Ask for the full test record. It should identify the meter number, type, size, test date, readings before and after testing, test volume, and error at each flow rate. Keep the record with the repair and billing documents.

A sudden increase doesn't automatically mean the tenant overused water. It also doesn't automatically mean the meter's defective. Location, test results, and notice dates decide who pays.
